output.title: When bookkeeping habits stop helping
output.body:
Some bookkeeping habits are useful. The limit shows up when a routine starts consuming the owner’s attention without changing the decision. At that point, “being organised” can quietly turn into manual labour with a neat label.

For a small business, the real question is not “Should I automate bookkeeping?” It is narrower: which one repeating bookkeeping task keeps showing up, has a clear input and output, and blocks higher-value work? Think invoice data entry, expense categorisation, or a reconciliation flag that needs the same yes/no or category decision every time. If the work is scan-heavy or OCR-dependent, that is a different case; Bareni currently keeps those out of scope.

A simple self-check is enough. Pick one bookkeeping task and write three lines: the input, the decision rule, and the output. For example: “invoice lands in email” → “route by vendor and description” → “line added to the expense sheet.” That is only an illustrative test, not a promise that automation fits. If you cannot write those three lines cleanly, the task is probably not bounded enough for a build yet.

If you can write them, you have a better basis for choosing between manual work, hiring help, or a small automation. That choice stays with the owner. Money movement and other high-risk decisions should remain human. And if a system is built, Bareni’s stated policy is that the customer owns the data, tool accounts, and code from the start. No one needs another clever bookkeeping habit that turns into a hobby.
